# AI-Driven Game Engines and Development Tools: Survey of Related Efforts

We surveyed recent projects and research in AI-assisted game engine creation, build automation, multi-API rendering, programmatic UI, and runtime-renderer flexibility.  Notable examples include commercial and open-source initiatives. Table 1 compares **Purge of the Crescent Veil (PoCV)** with other efforts across key dimensions. Subsequent sections describe each domain, citing documented work (GitHub repos, academic papers, blog posts) and noting areas where no AI-based solutions are known.

&#x20;*Figure 1: Dreamlab web-based game engine editor (collaborative, TypeScript) with AI-assisted coding and asset generation.*

## AI-Driven / AI-Assisted Game Engine Creation

* **Dreamlab (WorldQL)**: An open-source, Deno/TypeScript web game engine emphasizing multiplayer. Dreamlab supports real-time collaboration and “has a built-in AI assistant that helps you write code for your game or generate assets”. The engine requires no downloads (runs in-browser) and provides modern features (physics, networking, etc.). Its development blog details AI integration and an editor UI (Figure 1).
* **PlumAI (Jane Doe/John Smith)**: A newly open-sourced fork of Godot Engine featuring **AI-powered tools**. PlumAI “enhances 2D and 3D game development” with AI that “automates routine tasks, optimizes performance, and offers intelligent suggestions”. It targets rapid prototyping and exports to multiple platforms. PlumAI is MIT-licensed and community-driven.
* **GameNGen (Google Research)**: A research project demonstrating a **neural-model game engine**. The arXiv paper describes GameNGen as *“the first game engine powered entirely by a neural model”*, using a fast diffusion model to simulate games in real-time. In demos it can generate playable DOOM-like levels from text prompts at \~20 fps. This represents cutting-edge generative-AI as an engine backend.
* **Jabali / Project Makina**: (Industry startup) Building an AI-native engine/authoring tool (no-code/low-code) for games. Public info is limited to press: e.g. founders and venture funding, but detailed methods are unpublished. The focus is on “generative AI game engine” capabilities akin to simplifying game creation (similar in goal to Dreamlab/GameNGen).
* **Academic work (e.g. ZAGII)**: Some research (e.g. *ZAGII Engine*) explores AI in RPG engines (NPC reasoning, emergent narratives).  However, these focus on in-game AI/NPC behavior rather than automated engine code generation or build orchestration.

**Summary:**  Several projects (Dreamlab, PlumAI, GameNGen) push AI-assistance in engine development, but each has a narrower scope. Dreamlab and PlumAI integrate AI for code and design assistance within a traditional engine. GameNGen replaces much of the engine with a learned model. PoCV’s scope appears to combine all these elements (AI-generated engine code, multi-API support, build automation, etc.), which is more ambitious than any single existing project.

## AI-Autonomous Build Repair & Dependency Management

* **bumpgen (GitHub)**: An AI agent (GPT-4 based) that **updates npm packages**. It statically analyzes a Node project and automatically applies fixes for breaking changes when upgrading libraries. This open-source tool demonstrates AI rewriting code for build repairs.
* **EdgeBit Dependency Autofix**: Commercial platform for vulnerability and dependency management. Its “Dependency Autofix” analyzes a codebase’s call graph and dependency graph, then suggests upgrades.  Per documentation, *“AI is used to augment this determination by parsing how specific functions have changed”* in different versions. In other words, it uses AI to help decide safe dependency updates.
* **Project Thoth (Red Hat)**: A cloud-based **Python dependency resolver** using machine learning. Thoth’s solver uses reinforcement learning to find compatible package versions and can enforce custom criteria (performance, security, etc.) during resolution. This ML-driven resolver contrasts with traditional pip backtracking.
* **Other tools**: GitHub’s Dependabot or Azure DevOps may incorporate AI hints, but no documented system fully automates cross-repo build fixes via generative models (aside from niche tools like bumpgen).

**Summary:** AI-assisted tooling for builds and deps is emerging. Bumpgen and Thoth show AI can help upgrade packages, while enterprise tools like EdgeBit mix static analysis with ML. PoCV’s purported “autonomous build repair / bootstrap” capability goes beyond these by suggesting an AI that would automatically fix builds across multiple languages or platforms; we found no direct analogue that handles, for example, C++ build graph repair or multi-language bootstrap entirely via AI.

## AI-Generated Multi-Backend Rendering Support

* **bgfx (Branimir Karadzic)**: A widely-used **C++ rendering library** that abstracts graphics APIs. bgfx manually supports Direct3D 11/12, Metal, OpenGL/Vulkan, WebGL, etc.. It requires manual implementation of render paths for each backend, but it is not AI-driven.
* **Vk (MoltenVK/ANGLE, DXVK, etc.)**: These projects translate between APIs (e.g. OpenGL-over-Vulkan) at runtime, but all are hand-coded.
* **AI-Scaffolded Backends?** We found **no published tool or paper** where an AI generates or scaffolds multi-API rendering support. In existing multi-API engines (bgfx, Unity, Unreal), the bindings for each API are manually written. PoCV claims “multibackend rendering support generated by AI”; this appears **novel**, as there are no known precedents of automated code generation for multiple graphics APIs.
* **GPGPU/Shader ML?** Some research uses ML to optimize shaders, but not to automate whole renderer pipelines across APIs.

**Summary:** The idea of an AI automatically creating or abstracting rendering backends for OpenGL, DX11/12, Vulkan, RTX, etc. is not found in literature. The state of the art remains manual multi-backend libraries (e.g. bgfx). If PoCV’s claim holds (AI generating a unified backend), that would be unprecedented in published work.

## AI-Driven Programmatic UI Generation

* **AI2UI (GitHub)**: A React/Next.js tool that generates UI components via ChatGPT. The user enters a prompt, and the system “generates almost any UI components with OpenAI’s ChatGPT”, returning HTML/React/Tailwind code that can be directly used.
* **v0.diy (GitHub)**: An open-source “AI UI Generator” (alternative to v0.dev). It takes text or image prompts and produces frontend code for various frameworks (React, NextUI, etc.), using multiple AI models under the hood. The README highlights multi-provider support (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) and export to live code in frameworks.
* **Microsoft Sketch2Code**: An Azure AI Lab project where a CV model turns hand-drawn UI mockups into HTML wireframes. This uses computer vision (object detection + OCR) to identify buttons/text in an image and outputs HTML. It shows AI-generated UI code, though from images.
* **Avion Mission UI Generator**: A small open-source demo using Google Gemini. It builds a web UI from a simple prompt (e.g. a component spec). Stars: 7. Shows that even early LLMs can produce JSX/CSS from text.
* **Others**: Commercial tools like Uizard or Visily use AI to propose UI layouts from text/images, but detailed methods are proprietary. GitHub Copilot can assist with UI code, but is manual-invoked.

**Summary:** AI tools for UI code generation are active research and startup areas. Several open-source projects (AI2UI, v0.diy) allow programmatic UI creation from text. Industry examples (Sketch2Code, Uizard) demonstrate viability. PoCV’s claim of *“fully programmatic UI generation (no external assets) via AI”* overlaps these efforts. Its novelty would lie in end-to-end pipeline integration rather than UI code alone.

## Runtime-Injected / Dynamically Switchable Render Architectures

* **Traditional engines**: Modern engines like Unity or Unreal have configurable or scriptable render pipelines, but switching usually requires manual setup or editor changes. For example, Unity allows swapping between Built-in, URP, HDRP at runtime via script, but this is a built-in feature, not AI-driven.
* **Dynamic injection**: We found no examples of an AI dynamically injecting or altering rendering pipelines at runtime. Any switching today is either done in-editor or via straightforward code (e.g. assigning a new `RenderPipelineAsset` in Unity).
* **Adaptive architectures**: Research on runtime graphics reconfiguration exists (e.g. dynamic resolution scaling, shader substitution), but again no AI agent that “injects” entire subsystems.

**Summary:** The ability to automatically inject or swap rendering backends at run-time remains unaddressed by current tools. Unity’s manual pipeline switching is the closest analogue, and it is entirely developer-driven. PoCV’s implied goal of “runtime-injected rendering architectures” has no known prior art. This is a clear gap where PoCV’s approach would be novel.

## Novelty and Unsolved Areas

Based on available literature and code, several PoCV claims are **unprecedented**:

* **AI-generated multi-API backend:**  We found *no* framework where an LLM or generative model automatically creates multi-renderer support (OpenGL, DX, Vulkan, RTX, etc.). Existing cross-API libraries (bgfx) are hand-written. Automated scaffolding of this kind appears to be unsolved.
* **AI-based dynamic pipeline injection:** No documented system lets an AI reconfigure or inject render pipelines at runtime. Current engines require explicit developer steps (e.g. Unity’s C# switch). Dynamic swapping purely via AI is novel.
* **Integrated end-to-end AI engine/bootstrapping:** While individual pieces exist (AI code assist, AI dependency resolution, AI UI code), no single project covers all simultaneously. PoCV aims to combine AI creation of core engine code, build automation, multi-backend render generation, UI generation, and runtime flexibility. The combination of all these “AI factory” aspects is, to our knowledge, unique.

In summary, we identified several projects with overlapping goals (Dreamlab, PlumAI, GameNGen in engines; bumpgen, Thoth, EdgeBit in builds; AI2UI, v0.diy, Sketch2Code in UI).  Where possible, sources are cited above. However, key PoCV ambitions – especially multi-backend code generation and runtime architecture injection via AI – have no clear precedent in public work, marking them as novel or open problems.

**Sources:**  See citations above (academic, industry blogs, GitHub repositories). Each claim about project capabilities is backed by the cited source. Uncited or “none found” areas reflect absence of documented solutions in our research.

* **Other tools**: GitHub’s Dependabot or Azure DevOps may incorporate AI hints, but no documented system fully automates cross-repo build fixes via generative models (aside from niche tools like bumpgen).

**Summary:** AI-assisted tooling for builds and deps is emerging. Bumpgen and Thoth show AI can help upgrade packages, while enterprise tools like EdgeBit mix static analysis with ML. PoCV’s purported “autonomous build repair / bootstrap” capability goes beyond these by suggesting an AI that would automatically fix builds across multiple languages or platforms; we found no direct analogue that handles, for example, C++ build graph repair or multi-language bootstrap entirely via AI.

## AI-Generated Multi-Backend Rendering Support

* **bgfx (Branimir Karadzic)**: A widely-used **C++ rendering library** that abstracts graphics APIs. bgfx manually supports Direct3D 11/12, Metal, OpenGL/Vulkan, WebGL, etc.. It requires manual implementation of render paths for each backend, but it is not AI-driven.
* **Vk (MoltenVK/ANGLE, DXVK, etc.)**: These projects translate between APIs (e.g. OpenGL-over-Vulkan) at runtime, but all are hand-coded.
* **AI-Scaffolded Backends?** We found **no published tool or paper** where an AI generates or scaffolds multi-API rendering support. In existing multi-API engines (bgfx, Unity, Unreal), the bindings for each API are manually written. PoCV claims “multibackend rendering support generated by AI”; this appears **novel**, as there are no known precedents of automated code generation for multiple graphics APIs.
* **GPGPU/Shader ML?** Some research uses ML to optimize shaders, but not to automate whole renderer pipelines across APIs.

**Summary:** The idea of an AI automatically creating or abstracting rendering backends for OpenGL, DX11/12, Vulkan, RTX, etc. is not found in literature. The state of the art remains manual multi-backend libraries (e.g. bgfx). If PoCV’s claim holds (AI generating a unified backend), that would be unprecedented in published work.

## AI-Driven Programmatic UI Generation

* **AI2UI (GitHub)**: A React/Next.js tool that generates UI components via ChatGPT. The user enters a prompt, and the system “generates almost any UI components with OpenAI’s ChatGPT”, returning HTML/React/Tailwind code that can be directly used.
* **v0.diy (GitHub)**: An open-source “AI UI Generator” (alternative to v0.dev). It takes text or image prompts and produces frontend code for various frameworks (React, NextUI, etc.), using multiple AI models under the hood. The README highlights multi-provider support (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) and export to live code in frameworks.
* **Microsoft Sketch2Code**: An Azure AI Lab project where a CV model turns hand-drawn UI mockups into HTML wireframes. This uses computer vision (object detection + OCR) to identify buttons/text in an image and outputs HTML. It shows AI-generated UI code, though from images.
* **Avion Mission UI Generator**: A small open-source demo using Google Gemini. It builds a web UI from a simple prompt (e.g. a component spec). Stars: 7. Shows that even early LLMs can produce JSX/CSS from text.
* **Others**: Commercial tools like Uizard or Visily use AI to propose UI layouts from text/images, but detailed methods are proprietary. GitHub Copilot can assist with UI code, but is manual-invoked.

**Summary:** AI tools for UI code generation are active research and startup areas. Several open-source projects (AI2UI, v0.diy) allow programmatic UI creation from text. Industry examples (Sketch2Code, Uizard) demonstrate viability. PoCV’s claim of *“fully programmatic UI generation (no external assets) via AI”* overlaps these efforts. Its novelty would lie in end-to-end pipeline integration rather than UI code alone.

## Runtime-Injected / Dynamically Switchable Render Architectures

* **Traditional engines**: Modern engines like Unity or Unreal have configurable or scriptable render pipelines, but switching usually requires manual setup or editor changes. For example, Unity allows swapping between Built-in, URP, HDRP at runtime via script, but this is a built-in feature, not AI-driven.
* **Dynamic injection**: We found no examples of an AI dynamically injecting or altering rendering pipelines at runtime. Any switching today is either done in-editor or via straightforward code (e.g. assigning a new `RenderPipelineAsset` in Unity).
* **Adaptive architectures**: Research on runtime graphics reconfiguration exists (e.g. dynamic resolution scaling, shader substitution), but again no AI agent that “injects” entire subsystems.

**Summary:** The ability to automatically inject or swap rendering backends at run-time remains unaddressed by current tools. Unity’s manual pipeline switching is the closest analogue, and it is entirely developer-driven. PoCV’s implied goal of “runtime-injected rendering architectures” has no known prior art. This is a clear gap where PoCV’s approach would be novel.

## Novelty and Unsolved Areas

Based on available literature and code, several PoCV claims are **unprecedented**:

* **AI-generated multi-API backend:**  We found *no* framework where an LLM or generative model automatically creates multi-renderer support (OpenGL, DX, Vulkan, RTX, etc.). Existing cross-API libraries (bgfx) are hand-written. Automated scaffolding of this kind appears to be unsolved.
* **AI-based dynamic pipeline injection:** No documented system lets an AI reconfigure or inject render pipelines at runtime. Current engines require explicit developer steps (e.g. Unity’s C# switch). Dynamic swapping purely via AI is novel.
* **Integrated end-to-end AI engine/bootstrapping:** While individual pieces exist (AI code assist, AI dependency resolution, AI UI code), no single project covers all simultaneously. PoCV aims to combine AI creation of core engine code, build automation, multi-backend render generation, UI generation, and runtime flexibility. The combination of all these “AI factory” aspects is, to our knowledge, unique.

In summary, we identified several projects with overlapping goals (Dreamlab, PlumAI, GameNGen in engines; bumpgen, Thoth, EdgeBit in builds; AI2UI, v0.diy, Sketch2Code in UI).  Where possible, sources are cited above. However, key PoCV ambitions – especially multi-backend code generation and runtime architecture injection via AI – have no clear precedent in public work, marking them as novel or open problems.

**Sources:**  See citations above (academic, industry blogs, GitHub repositories). Each claim about project capabilities is backed by the cited source. Uncited or “none found” areas reflect absence of documented solutions in our research.
